transcript:
[09:00] Meeting start
Host: Maya Chen (Redwood AE)
Attendees listed on the header. Duration approx 55 min.

[09:01] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[09:01] Sara: Sara here.
[09:02] Tom: Tom here.
[09:02] Ravi: Ravi here.
[09:02] Elena: Elena here.
[09:02] Liam: Liam from Redwood here.
[09:03] Maya: Great. Today we want to go over the cost/unit economics experiments we ran, look at tokens per second per dollar, and decide on batching/caching defaults for the rest of the pilot.

[09:04] Liam: Quick recap - we ran three configs last week: batch sizes 1, 8, and 16; prefix caching enabled vs disabled; and two quant modes: fp16 and q4_0. The headline: batching improves throughput but increases p95 latency for tail requests, caching gives the largest cost savings for repeated prefixes.

[09:05] Ravi: Can you share the tokens/sec per dollar numbers? The spreadsheet I saw had a few columns but some numbers didn't match our traffic.

[09:06] Maya: Sure, Liam, can you pull up the slide? (brief pause) Okay, for redwood-7b-q4_0 with prefix cache hit rate ~40% and batch=8 we saw about 12,500 tokens/sec per GPU-hour, which translates to ~0.012 tokens/sec/$ on the hosted pricing example - I think the wording in the sheet is confusing, but that's the normalized number. With batch=1 and no cache it's ~4,100 tokens/sec per GPU-hour.

[09:07] Tom: Sorry, hold on - tokens/sec per GPU-hour vs tokens/sec per dollar - are we normalizing to our committed price? Our Dedicated pricing is a different curve.

[09:08] Maya: Good clarification. The numbers Liam quoted are per-GPU-hour raw throughput. We then applied the committed hourly rate from your dedicated quote to get tokens/sec/$. For quick comparison, the spreadsheet has both columns: raw tokens/sec/GPU-hour and tokens/sec/$.

[09:09] Liam: I'll put it simply: with caching on and a 40% hit rate, cost per 1M tokens dropped by ~36% in our tests. Caching + q4 quantization together gave the best unit economics while keeping median latency under your SLO. But p95 increases when batch>8 on our infra for long-tail requests.

[09:11] Ravi: That 40% hit rate - how representative is that of our traffic? Our prefix reuse for completion tasks is high, but for chat it's lower.

[09:11] Elena: Right, our chat workload has a lot of unique prefixes. We ran a quick histogram and saw ~18% reuse for full chat sessions but higher for assistant prompts.

[09:12] Liam: That's expected. The savings are workload dependent; for mainly completion / instruction-following tasks you'll see bigger wins. For your mixed workload the spreadsheet projects ~22% net hit rate and ~18% cost savings compared to no cache.

[09:13] Sara: Can you show the latency breakdown? We care about p95 tail for user-facing features.

[09:14] Nia: (shares screen) Here's the per-route dashboard - median for batch=4 hovers at 120ms, p95 at 310ms. Batch=8 pushes p95 to 420ms because batching queues a few requests to fill the batch. If you want consistent p95 < 300ms, we recommend targeting batch=4 and optimizing queueing windows.

[09:15] Tom: So batch=4 seems like a sweet spot for our SLOs. What about throughput? Will we lose too much cost efficiency?

[09:16] Liam: Tradeoff math: batch=4 gives ~18% less tokens/sec than batch=8 but improves p95 ~26%. With quantization q4, the memory footprint drops enough to host more concurrent workers per GPU, recovering some throughput. Net cost impact depends on cache hit rate: with 25% hit rate batch=4 + cache + q4 is still ~20% cheaper than baseline no-cache fp16 batch=1.

[09:18] Ravi: Did you test dynamic batching with latency-aware thresholds? We have some beams of high priority where p95 must be low.

[09:19] Liam: Yes - we did a small run using dynamic batching with a 60ms wait window for low-latency routes and 150ms for background routes. It preserves p95 on high-priority while letting background requests batch. Implementation detail: Redwood's routing rules let you set per-route batching windows and fallbacks to smaller models if latency spikes.

[09:20] Elena: How stable is q4 quantization for our prompts? Any quality regressions?

[09:21] Maya: We ran evals on your validation prompt set. Average log-prob drop was small; in about 3% of prompts we saw minor fluency issues. We flagged those in the eval spreadsheet. If you need zero-regression we recommend running side-by-side A/B traffic to measure user impact before switching fully.

[09:22] Ravi: Can we get a list of the prompts that regressed? We need to check for sampling artifacts.

[09:22] Liam: We'll share the eval rows with sample outputs. Note transcription here: some proper nouns got scrambled in earlier exports (redwood names etc) - but the sample outputs are in the linked sheet.

[09:23] Sara: On caching - do we need to change our client code to get prefix caching to work?

[09:24] Nia: Minimal changes: you annotate requests with a prefix_id and set cacheable=true for deterministic completions. For chat state you can store conversational KV keys; Redwood's SDK supports automatic prefix hashing. We'll send a code snippet.

[09:25] Tom: Any impact on privacy/compliance when we store prefixes? We can't send PII to shared caches.

[09:26] Maya: Important point. For hosted pilots we'd recommend encryption at rest and KMS-managed keys; you can opt out of global cache and use dedicated per-tenant cache on Dedicated or Private deployments. We have an SSO/security docs link in the follow-ups.

[09:28] Ravi: Can you remind me of the expected cost delta if we move to Dedicated vs Hosted for this workload?

[09:28] Liam: For your committed Dedicated quote, base hourly is lower but you take on utilization risk. In the spreadsheet we modeled committed 70% utilization - that yields ~30% lower unit cost vs hosted. If utilization drops to 40% the math flips. We included a sensitivity table in the sheet.

[09:30] Sara: It sounds like caching and dedicated capacity together deliver the best unit economics, but we need to be confident in hit rates and utilization.

[09:31] Maya: Agreed. So action plan: you run a 24-hour baseline with caching enabled to confirm hit rates and CPU/GPU utilization. We'll in parallel run a throughput SLO test with batch=4 and dynamic batching on high-priority routes.

[09:33] Tom: For the SLO test, what's the target traffic shape? We want to simulate peak day (2x baseline) and steady state.

[09:34] Liam: We'll provide a template traffic trace generator and default parameters - we're also happy to replay your uploaded trace.

[09:35] Ravi: One more thing on batching: is there a way to prioritize certain client tokens to avoid waiting in the batch? e.g., websocket low-latency users.

[09:36] Nia: Yes, priority routing supports per-request priority headers; high-priority requests skip batching windows or use lower-wait thresholds. That will slightly raise cost for those requests but preserves UX.

[09:37] Sara: Ok, let's talk timing. When can we expect the cost spreadsheet and the recommended config?

[09:38] Maya: We'll send the updated spreadsheet and the recommended config & code samples by Friday (2025-04-25). Liam will follow up with the exact model variant and quant settings by Thursday (2025-04-24).

[09:39] Ravi: We'll try to upload the 2-hour production trace by Wednesday the 30th and run the 24-hour baseline ASAP.

[09:40] Elena: Also request: can Redwood include a small benchmark of tokens/sec/$ using our committed price so we can show finance?

[09:41] Liam: Yes - we'll add a committed-utilization sensitivity table and a one-page summary for finance.

[09:43] Maya: Quick recap and next steps?

[09:43] Sara: Great meeting, that matches our notes.

[09:44] Maya: Recap: Redwood sends updated cost model + config samples + eval outputs; customer uploads trace and runs cache-enabled baseline; schedule SLO benchmark week of 2025-05-05.

[09:45] Tom: One last question - are there any recommended A/B experiment templates for switching quant modes live?

[09:46] Liam: Yes, we have an A/B rollout template in the pilot docs: run 5-10% traffic to q4 variant for 24-72h, track quality metrics and business KPIs, then gradually increase. We'll link that doc.

[09:47] Maya: Perfect. Anything else?

[09:48] (brief crosstalk)

[09:49] Sara: Nothing else from me.

[09:50] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email with the sheet and invites.

[09:51] Meeting end
